analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit for seniors, funded by higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 1999, referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let every Medicare beneficiary buy outpatient prescription drug coverage through a private insurance policy, a Medicare managed-care plan, or an employer plan, with federal subsidies covering 100% of the premium for seniors with incomes below 150% of the poverty line, a sliding share up to 175%, and 25% for everyone else. The money would come from a dedicated fund fed by sharply higher federal tobacco taxes and from the budget surplus. It banned pre-existing condition exclusions and required appeal rights when a drug was left off a plan's approved list.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries without drug coverage — especially low-income seniors, whose premiums would be fully paid — gain access to prescription drug coverage with guaranteed issue, no pre-existing condition exclusions, and appeal rights for non-formulary drugs.

how_it_helps.text: All Medicare beneficiaries entitled to hospital benefits and enrolled in medical insurance would be given access to outpatient prescription drug coverage through a Medigap policy, a Medicare+Choice plan, or a group health plan.
Financial assistance would cover 100% of the premium cost for beneficiaries with incomes at or below 150% of the poverty line, taper down to 175%, and cover 25% for all other beneficiaries.
Coverage could not apply pre-existing condition exclusions, and any formulary would need an appeals process for medically necessary drugs plus 60 days' advance notice before changing the drug list.
The program would be financed by a dedicated trust fund drawing on new tobacco excise tax revenue and amounts appropriated from the on-budget surplus.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers and tobacco companies, through much higher federal excise taxes — the cigarette tax would rise from $12 to $44.50 per thousand in 2000-2001 and $47 thereafter — plus taxpayers generally, through the use of the on-budget surplus.

drawbacks.text: Financing rests on tobacco excise taxes, which are paid by smokers; the cigarette tax would rise from $12 to $44.50 per thousand in 2000-2001 and $47.00 thereafter, with parallel increases on cigars, smokeless tobacco, and pipe tobacco. Because lower-income people smoke at higher rates, this is a regressive way to fund a senior benefit.

Most beneficiaries above the low-income thresholds would receive only a 25% subsidy, leaving them to pay three-quarters of the premium themselves — which the bill's own affordability study acknowledges as an open question.

If the trust fund proved insufficient, the bill required automatic retrenchment: the standard subsidy could be cut to as low as 10%, income thresholds lowered, and assistance suspended entirely for a year.

Participation is voluntary for insurers as well as beneficiaries — no Medicare+Choice plan or Medigap issuer is required to offer the coverage — so access would depend on companies choosing to participate, and beneficiaries who delayed enrolling would face reduced assistance.
Coverage would be delivered through private policies and plans rather than a direct Medicare benefit, keeping private insurers as the middlemen for a publicly subsidized benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well-targeted at the poorest seniors, who would pay nothing, and the consumer protections (guaranteed issue, no pre-existing condition exclusions, appeal rights) are meaningful. But the design has serious weaknesses: the regressive tobacco-tax financing shifts costs onto low-income smokers, the 25% subsidy for middle-income seniors may be too small to make coverage affordable, and the automatic-sunset mechanism means the benefit could shrink or vanish if costs outran revenue. A directly administered Medicare drug benefit with broader subsidies would have delivered the same help with fewer of those risks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Ways and Means and Commerce committees, which referred it to their health subcommittees, and it sat there with no hearings, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) introduced the SPICE Act on August 5, 1999, joined by Rep. Marge Roukema (R-NJ).
The Speaker referred the bill to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Commerce Committee, a split reflecting that it touched both Medicare financing and insurance regulation.
On August 19 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and on September 15 to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action was ever taken, and the bill died with the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001.
The bill drew only three cosponsors total — one Republican and two Democrats — and no votes were ever taken on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies avoided the large excise tax increases that would have funded the benefit, and private insurers and Medicare plans faced no new coverage requirements. Seniors without drug coverage remained without it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a small bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic sponsor with one Republican and two Democratic cosponsors — but with only four backers and no votes ever taken, no partisan pattern in support or opposition can be measured.

industries.note: The bill's funding mechanism raises federal tobacco excise taxes sharply — cigarettes from $12 to $44.50 per thousand in 2000-2001 and $47 after — and restricts importation of previously exported products. Tobacco companies and their customers would have borne the cost of the senior drug benefit.

The bill makes private insurers the permanent channel for subsidized senior drug coverage: federal subsidies are paid directly to policy issuers, and a new standardized drug-only Medigap policy would be sold only through board-approved issuers. Insurers gain a subsidized customer base, though they must accept guaranteed issue and benefit rules.
Plans offering the drug coverage would receive federal subsidy payments for their enrollees, adding subsidized revenue. The bill forbids payments to plans that cherry-pick healthy beneficiaries.

A new subsidized drug benefit would add millions of insured customers with no government price negotiation in the bill. The industry bears some cost containment, since plans may use formularies and generic substitution, but the main effect is expanded insured demand paid for by taxes.
